one_line: Blood-based biomarkers, particularly plasma p-tau217, offer a highly accurate, cost-effective alternative to PET and CSF for diagnosing and predicting Alzheimer's disease in clinical and trial settings.
summary: This review evaluates the current state and future clinical implementation of blood-based biomarkers (BBMs) for Alzheimer's disease (AD). The authors highlight that high-performing assays for plasma phosphorylated tau (especially p-tau217) exhibit diagnostic accuracy comparable to established CSF and PET imaging methods. While plasma Aβ42/Aβ40 ratios show limited robustness in routine clinical settings due to small effect sizes, plasma p-tau assays are highly robust and can accurately predict future cognitive decline even in preclinical stages. The integration of BBMs is poised to revolutionize clinical trial recruitment by prescreening for amyloid positivity, significantly reducing costs and time associated with PET scans. The authors argue that while global standardization and prospective real-world validations in diverse populations are still needed, BBMs will soon enable primary care physicians to accurately diagnose and manage AD.

key_claims.claim: Plasma p-tau217 assays show high diagnostic accuracy for distinguishing AD from other neurodegenerative diseases.
key_claims.evidence: p-tau217 is the tau variant that shows the largest fold increase in individuals with symptomatic AD, with increases of about 300–700% compared to healthy individuals and patients with other neurodegenerative diseases.
key_claims.location: BBMs for diagnosis and prognosis of cognitively impaired patients in specialist memory clinics

key_claims.claim: The plasma Aβ42/Aβ40 ratio has low robustness for routine clinical settings.
key_claims.evidence: A very modest drop of 8–15% in symptomatic AD, combined with analytical variability, results in poor robustness compared to CSF equivalents.
key_claims.location: BBMs for diagnosis and prognosis of cognitively impaired patients in specialist memory clinics

key_claims.claim: Prescreening with blood biomarkers significantly improves clinical trial efficiency for preclinical AD.
key_claims.evidence: Notes the A4 trial required 3.5 years and >4,000 amyloid PET scans to identify 1,169 participants; using high-performing BBMs early in enrollment greatly reduces the number of required PET/CSF investigations.
key_claims.location: BBMs as prescreening biomarkers in clinical trials

limitations: Clinical cutoffs and diagnostic performance metrics predominantly rely on retrospective, batch-analyzed studies rather than real-world prospective testing.
Lack of analytical standardization and certified reference materials for blood-based biomarkers across different laboratories.
Performance and cutoffs in diverse primary care populations with multiple comorbidities require further prospective validation.
red_flags: Substantial financial conflicts of interest among all authors, including direct patents for p-tau217 assays (J.D.) and company ownership (Brain Biomarker Solutions by K.B. and H.Z.), which may introduce bias favoring the adoption of these specific biomarkers.
